HSCT THERAPY FOR MS

By: Chwayitisa Futshane | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

Unique Selling Point:
HSCT or Hematopioetic Stem Cell Transplant, is to date the only scientifically proven treatment that STOPS underlying disease progression in all types of MS and restores normal immune self-tolerance and produces lasting curative symptomatic improvement for the majority of MS patients. It is not a new procedure as such, as it has been used to treat cancer since the 1960’s, but it is a relatively new treatment for MS.
The term multiple sclerosis means ‘many scars’. Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an unpredictable, often disabling disease of the central nervous system that disrupts the flow of information within the brain, and between the brain and body.
MS symptoms vary widely and include blurred vision, weak limbs, tingling sensations, unsteadiness and fatigue. For some people, MS is characterised by periods of relapse and remission while, for others, it has a progressive pattern. For everyone with MS, it makes life unpredictable.
With the treatment of HSCT for MS, comes the hope of stopping the progression of the disease and the opportunity of looking forward to a future. MS has no known cause/s as yet. There is no drug that can cure MS.
HSCT as a treatment for MS, was discovered by chance by Dr Burt at North Western University, Chicago. He started HSCT treatment back in 1996. He noticed that the leukemia patients he was treating needed to be “re-vaccinated” because the protection from childhood diseases like the measles and mumps was being lost. The cells affected by transfusion treatments were losing the “memory” of these original childhood vaccinations. He started with trials in the lab to see if this treatment would be successful for autoimmune diseases and it worked. Then the FDA approved the procedure of adult stem cell therapy to be used on people suffering from Multiple Sclerosis.
HSCT treatment involves transplanting stem cells, in the hopes that the new cells won’t have the properties that caused the body to attack itself and will create healthy new cells. Before the transplant, patients are given a high dose of an immunosuppressant regimen for six days.
There is no ethical dilemma as the treatment uses adult stem cells extracted from the patients own blood, and no embryonic stem cells are involved.

Press Release:


Multiple Sclerosis (MS) is a debilitating condition affecting the body’s nervous system and can lead to muscle spasms, chronic pain, depression and paralysis. It’s incurable but scientifically tested Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation (HSCT) is helping to halt the progression of the disease. HSCT has commonly been used as a cancer treatment, but has now also been found to be effective against various auto-immune diseases like MS.

Script:


HSCT THERAPY FOR MS
Commission: 5261

AUDIO DUR
V/O:
When Christelle Taute from Belville in the Western Cape was diagnosed with Multiple Sclerosis or MS in 2000, she was devastated.
7
CHRISTELLE:
I was like, I am only twenty-nine so what does this mean for the rest of my life. And I started crying. I think the immediate reaction of many people who get diagnosed with MS is “I am going to be in a wheelchair”.
V/O:
It started with an episode of optic neuritis, inflammation of the optic nerve and often one of the first symptoms people with MS experience.
8
CHRISTELLE:
When I looked at your face, I would could see your hair and chin. I could not see the middle part, it was greyed out.
V/O:
The condition was temporary and the progression of MS slowed down. Then two years later she suddenly began to experience pins and needles in her fingers.
8
CHRISTELLE:
Until about 2008 I was still the girl on the dance floor at the wedding. I then started feeling quite weak in the way that I walked. Slowly it happened. Eventually it is weird, you just can’t walk anymore.
V/O:
Over time, Christelle began losing her independence, struggling to take care of herself. When her partner is away on business, she is dependent on friends or neighbours.
9
CHRISTELLE:
When I transfer from the wheelchair to the bed for example and I fall down on the flour, there is no way that I can get up. I phoned my neighbour once and said, “Will you please come and do the electricity reading and while you are here, will you please pick me up from the floor?”
V/O:
For Werner Hamann, a young lawyer from Pretoria, the first signs of Multiple Sclerosis came without warning while he was cycling in 2014.
8
WERNER:
My left leg did not want to work. I tried to step on the bicycle pedals and it just did not want to go around. It slipped, every time it slipped.
V/O:
Werner was a very active person and for him MS progressed much faster, especially within the last two years and within months he had trouble walking.
9
WERNER:
It went from normal, to bad to worse.
LINK:
The central nervous system links everything the body does and the specific symptoms that appear with MS depends on which part of the central nervous system is affected and the job of that particular nerve. That is why MS is different for everyone.
V/O:
MS has perplexed medical experts for decades because the cause is unknown, and the disease - incurable.

Now, scientifically proven Hemapoietic stem cell transplantation or HSCT, that’s been used for decades in the treatment of certain types of Leukaemia, is helping to halt the deterioration of the disease.
6

11
DR OPPERMAN:
There are many types of stem cell transplant and the only one that works for Multiple Sclerosis, at the moment, is Haemopoietic stem cell transplant.
V/O:
Dr Dion Opperman, a neurologist from Cape Town, explains that MS is an auto immune disorder where your own body attacks the central nervous system.
8
DR OPPERMAN:
And what we are basically doing is we are rebooting your immune system.
V/O:
As an auto-immune disease, MS can have a devastating impact on how the central nervous system functions.
6
DR OPPERMAN:
Your own body attacks your brain, basically. In this case it attacks the myelin in the central nervous system, in the brain and spinal cord.
V/O:
Myelin sheaths are sleeves of fatty tissue that protect your nerve cells. These cells are part of your central nervous system, which carries messages back and forth between your brain and the rest of your body.
12
DR OPPERMAN:
You have a nerve cell with an axon and the axon is covered in Myelin. Kind of like a Telkom cable with a copper wire and an insulator. So basically, what happens when you have an attack, you lose your insulator. The myelin comes off. And that is what happens and that is why the patients have symptoms.

CLAIRE:
So, what happens when there is no myelin?

DR OPPERMAN:
It shorts out like it would in a wire. So basically, the message comes to a point and it cannot go through because the myelin is there for the impulses to communicate from one axon to another.
V/O:
This is what a normal brain scan should look like. And these, are the damaged areas in the brain of an MS patient.

There are roughly two main groups of MS. Primary Progressive MS or PPM and Relapsing Remitting MS or RRM.
8

6
LINK:
In PPM the progress is slow and consistent without any improvement and with RRM there is a major incident or incidents that could show improvement but could later progress. They are managed completely differently currently.
DR OPPERMAN:
In SA we only have treatment for PPM currently. We put them on drugs, we monitor them clinically, we monitor them with MRI’s and make sure that there is no new inflammatory disease going on.
LINK:
That is until HSCR became an option for some patients! Dr David Brittain is one of the few haematologists in South Africa that performs HSCT for MS.
V/O:
The unit is located at Netcare Pretoria East Hospital.

In all sections staff apply strict infection control because they work with immuno-suppressed patients.
3

5

DR OPPERMAN:
We re-infuse a naive immune system, so it is like a baby’s immune system and does not recognise the body’s self and in this case the myelin sheath of the nerves as foreign and does not attack it any more.
V/O:
The first step in the treatment is an immuno-suppressive chemo therapy. It destroys the immune system but also stimulates the release of bone marrow stem cells into the blood for harvesting, in a process called apheresis.
12
DR BRITTAIN:
It is essentially a computerised centrifuge, or a milk creamer and we take the cream off the milk of the patients’ blood by circulating it through the centrifuge and sipping off the layer with the stem cells in and returning the rest of the blood to the patient.
V/O:
The stem cells are frozen and stored at minus one hundred and ninety-five degrees.

The patient is then given a second, conditioning regimen of chemotherapy that kills their immune system completely.
5

6
DR BRITTAIN:
But that chemo therapy also at the same time kills the person’s bone marrow and you need the bone marrow to make blood cells. So, then we infuse the stem cells that we previously harvested, and they grow and make the blood again but also a new immune system.
NON SMIT:
It makes me very excited. It is a procedure that we have now seen works.
V/O:
Non Smit is the Director of MS South Africa in the Western Cape, a movement that informs, supports and empowers people with MS. This support is crucial because MS not only affects the person with the disease.

13
NON:
You need a team. It affects the family, it affects your mind, it affects you cognitively. You get depression.
DR BRITTAIN:
To be faced with a disease that is not being controlled, and is slowly stealing who you are, both physically and mentally, is very depressing. And to have some hope is very encouraging and that is what we would like to do, is to give some patients hope.
V/O:
Christelle had her HSCT in 2015 and is optimistic that the deterioration of her disease was halted.

But after eighteen years, the damage to the nerves themselves means that Christelle will remain in a wheelchair.
6

6
CHRISTELLE:
It has stabilized so nothing became worse. But it stayed where it was at. I can’t walk, the message does not get to my legs.
V/O:
Werner had his HSCT only four weeks ago and is already feeling some improvement.
5
WERNER:
There are things that I can do. I can stand in the shower with my eyes closed washing my hair and my face without any problems.
DR BRITTAIN:
In people who have more recent onset and who have active disease it will halt the progress of the disease and in a significant proportion of people reverse it.
V/O:
In December, Werner will be getting married and he’s adamant about one thing…
5
CLAIRE:
So, tell us about walking down the aisle. Is that going to happen with or without the crutch?

WERNER:
I am going to walk without the crutch.










PROMO’S

Promo #1: 10 sec
Stem-cell therapy now halts the deterioration of Multiple Sclerosis, a devastating disease with no cause or cure, that affects sufferers physically and mentally. (10)



Promo #2: 15 sec
V/O:
Christelle Taute from Cape Town suffers from Multiple Sclerosis, but stem cell therapy prevented the disease from progressing. (7)

Christelle:
If I take the results that I had, I wish I could have had it earlier because maybe I could still have walked then. (8)



Promo # 3: 15 sec
V/O:
It’s scientifically tested and saving hundreds of lives around the world, but how does Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation halt the progression of multiple sclerosis? (8)

Dr Opperman:
We re-infuse a naive immune system, so we are basically rebooting the immune system. (8)






Promo #4: 30 sec
V/O:
When Christelle Taute was diagnosed with Multiple Sclerosis she was devastated. (4)
Christelle:
I was like, I am only twenty-nine so what does this mean for the rest of my life. (6)
V/O:
Stem cell treatment for MS, that had been used for decades to treat certain types of leukaemia, gave her hope. (3)
Dr Opperman:
What we are doing is we are basically rebooting your immune system. (3)
V/O:
After she had Haemopoietic stem cell treatment for MS three years ago, it halted the deterioration of the disease. (7)
Dr Brittain:
That is what we would like to do, is to give them some hope. (5)
